title: Does remote work hurt people starting out?

turns.speaker: Ellie
turns.text: We've lost three graduates in eighteen months and every one of them said the same thing on the way out. They felt invisible.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Invisible how? Were they being given work?

turns.speaker: Ellie
turns.text: Plenty of work. What they weren't getting was anyone noticing when they were stuck.

turns.speaker: Yusuf
turns.text: That's the bit remote is genuinely bad at. When I started, half of what I learned I learned by overhearing. Someone two desks away would be on the phone doing the thing I'd been guessing at all week.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: You can't overhear a video call.

turns.speaker: Yusuf
turns.text: No, and you can't ask a small question either. Everything becomes a meeting request, so you sit on it instead.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: I'd say the answer is deliberate structure rather than making everyone come back, though. If the learning used to happen by accident, and the accident's gone, you have to schedule it.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Pair them with someone senior for an hour a day and don't make it optional. That's not the same as the corridor, but it beats hoping.

turns.speaker: Ellie
turns.text: It's more expensive than the corridor was, mind you. Somebody's hour is being spent.

turns.speaker: Yusuf
turns.text: It was always being spent. It just never appeared on anyone's calendar, so nobody costed it.

points: Ellie's team lost three graduates in eighteen months, all saying they felt invisible.
The problem was not a lack of work but that nobody noticed when they were stuck.
Yusuf argues remote work removes incidental learning, since much early knowledge comes from overhearing colleagues.
He adds that small questions become meeting requests, so junior staff sit on them instead of asking.

Dana proposes deliberate structure rather than a return to the office: if learning used to happen by accident, it now has to be scheduled, for example daily pairing with a senior colleague, made compulsory.
Ellie notes this costs someone's time; Yusuf replies that the time was always being spent but never appeared on a calendar, so it was never counted.
